Persona AI wants to put a welder where the work is

Persona's welding-first approach connects scarce industrial labor, human tools and expert demonstrations to the job of building a useful humanoid service.

October 26, 202625 min read

roboticshumanoidsindustryrobot-learning

Imagine a shipyard with an order it could build and a seam waiting for a welder. The steel is there. The customer wants the ship. Hiring another capable person would help the yard move the work along, but the yard can't find enough people. A robot earns its place here by adding useful welding capacity.

That's the situation behind Persona AI's first job. The Houston company wants humanoids to do skilled industrial work with the tools people already use, beginning with welding in shipyards and steel shops. I prefer this initial market choice among the companies compared here. There's a specific customer problem to solve and a specific skill to learn. Following one seam through the proposed business makes the attraction easier to understand, along with the work Persona still has ahead of it.

The first job shapes the company

A humanoid's first job chooses much of its development environment. A warehouse gives it repeated material-handling work and a fleet operator who can count completed moves. A home puts it among everyday chores and a household deciding how much help to buy. Persona's choice puts a welding tool in its hand, an experienced operator in its learning loop, and a customer waiting for more production.

The map on the board places these choices alongside each other. Read the work and the evidence together. Agility has an operating tote count; Persona has shown a teleoperated weld. A reservation, a pilot agreement, and work already performed each answer a different question.

Agility's live material handling gives a customer a way to assess return on investment through actual workflow. Tote handling also has established conveyors and robot arms. Wheeled machines can serve that work too. At home, the purchase competes with other uses of a household budget. Persona is choosing a skilled job where scarce labor can hold up valuable output. These customer economics help explain why its initial scope appeals to me.

An unstaffed seam holds up output

In Evan Ackerman's IEEE Spectrum interview, co-founder Nic Radford describes industrial partners with substantial backlogs and too little labor. Persona's skilled-trades explanation makes the consequence concrete through an unwelded seam delaying a hull worth millions. That is the company's economic argument, with the seam standing between unfinished work and something the customer can sell.

Labor figures give this situation some scale. Biz New Orleans relays an American Welding Society projection of roughly 82,500 US welding jobs needing to be filled each year through 2029. It also gives an average working-welder age of about 55 and roughly two entrants for every five retiring.

On the board, keep the geography and dates attached to the other numbers. Persona's accounts put the skilled-worker shortfall in North American and Korean shipbuilding at roughly 40,000. Its Korean manufacturing account puts the average age on Ulsan yard production floors at 48.3 and reports yards turning down orders. A separate industry estimate relayed by Persona and trade press projects 2.1 million unfilled US manufacturing jobs by 2030. The source notes retain the other forecasts with their own horizons.

Consider the yard's next unstaffed seam. If a robot can do acceptable work there, the yard gains work it otherwise couldn't complete with its available crew. The relevant comparison includes the value of that additional production. Radford describes helping customers' “top line, not necessarily their bottom line”, and considers the possibility “even if our robot was more expensive than a human”. This is a hypothetical about the value of added capacity; it supplies neither a robot price nor a measured margin or saving.

The customer buys continuing labor

Persona's proposed transaction follows that reasoning. In a February 5, 2025 InnovationMap interview, Radford describes retaining ownership of the robots and selling labor, a robotics-as-a-service arrangement. The lease offering bundles the robot with AI platform updates, custom tooling modules and fleet management training. Persona calls itself “the labor platform for skilled industrial work”. Its modular-platform description reaches beyond the initial weld to fabrication and inspection, with construction and energy alongside shipyards and steel shops as target industries.

Follow the arrows in the board's service diagram. Labor goes to the customer and payment returns to Persona, while ownership stays with the supplier. For the yard, the proposition includes continued usefulness and support as the equipment learns and changes. For Persona, that makes keeping the machine useful part of the ongoing business. Radford wants customers whose locations could accommodate hundreds of robots; that's his desired customer scale.

Co-founder and chief technology officer Jerry Pratt connects the same customer value to engineering choices. In the IEEE interview, he argues that valuable industrial output permits more spending on robot quality and features. He expects home robots to face stronger competition and price pressure. An initial job therefore helps set an engineering budget as well as a sales pitch. The next question is whether welding gives that budget a tractable task.

A long seam contains repeated small motions

Welding combines skill with a useful constraint. For the task discussed in the IEEE interview, the metal's melt rate limits torch travel to roughly one centimeter per second. The motion at the torch involves repeated adjustments on the scale of millimeters. Radford describes hundreds of kilometers of linear welds per ship. The board abbreviates centimeters per second as cm/s and millimeters as mm; its long seam and small repeated motions show two scales of the same job.

Think through a deliberately simple example. At one centimeter per second, a one-meter seam takes about 100 seconds of travel, because a meter contains 100 centimeters. That's an illustrative calculation using the interview's task-specific rate. It excludes reaching the seam and every other part of the job. It explains why making a robot move its arm faster wouldn't by itself make this weld finish faster. The process gives the robot time in which it has to keep doing the small motion correctly.

Persona plans to start with common, relatively uncomplicated linear welds. Repeated, checkable motion offers a specific learning target. Picture a person on a twentieth similar seam and the concentration it takes to keep the motion consistent. The twentieth seam on the board illustrates that fatigue and boredom. A useful robot would carry that consistency through repeated work.

The hand still has a demanding job. Pratt says tool use is difficult, and Persona deliberately wants its robot to use the crew's existing tools. Grinders and plasma cutters are part of that ambition too. Keeping the same tools connects the manipulation problem to installation in an existing workplace. A special robot cell asks the site to accommodate the machinery; a machine using crew tools takes on more of that accommodation itself.

The robot has to reach the seam

The one-meter calculation began with the torch already in position. Radford's description of a shipyard makes reaching that position part of the problem. These are open-air sites a couple hundred meters long, with horizontal and vertical spars along the route. Work happens at ground level and overhead, sometimes through portholes. A ladder or a spar can be on the way to paid work.

The board puts a wheeled base beside a spar and a humanoid stepping across it. Wheels need a suitable route; legs offer a way to follow routes already used by welders. The porthole drawing carries the idea from locomotion into reach. In this setting the body is part of the installation argument. Retrofitting a yard around a robot can cost more than the robot itself, so the customer has to consider the changes needed to get the machine to its work.

That conclusion depends on the place. In the companion essay, I argue against legs in a flat without stairs. The yard supplies obstacles and work positions that change the comparison. It also supplies a serious integration problem. Crews already work around cranes, arc light and falling steel, and adding a biped requires further safety and class work. Persona's standards relationship enters the story below.

Expert control creates demonstrations on the robot

Now put an expert welder behind the robot. Persona's teleoperation lead explains the division of work in an August 6, 2026 company account. A person supplies intent and judgment through virtual reality, abbreviated VR, and motion capture. The robot supplies balance and locomotion, with its learned stack supporting foot placement and vision. The person can concentrate on the welding while the platform handles the bodily control needed to carry it out.

Trace the board's loop from the operator to the robot, then to the recordings. The expert's tool motion happens on the actual hardware in the conditions the system needs to handle. Arc light and smoke are part of the job; uneven floors are part of reaching it. Recording these sessions gives Persona demonstrations tied to those tools and conditions. The next step is to train a skill, test it, and use further demonstrations and tests to improve it.

Persona describes autonomy developing “one real task at a time”, supported by high-fidelity simulation and real-world testing. The IEEE account anticipates tens of thousands of hours of expert demonstrations. That is a planned collection scale. Persona's teleoperation account places general humanoid autonomy “further off than the headlines suggest”, while its team works on repeatable, usable operation, including what task 200 of a shift should feel like for an operator. The two-hundredth task is a reliability target in this account.

This puts the learning plan close to the first commercial job. The seam we started with can become an expert demonstration, then a task for the robot to carry out independently. While every weld requires an expert to drive it, the service remains teleoperation. Independence has to emerge from the training and testing for the proposed automation to add that capability.

Different first jobs supply different learning material. Agility's path runs through live logistics, NEO's through homes, and Apollo's through fleets collecting data with Google DeepMind. In the Figure, Generalist and Physical Intelligence essay, Figure pretrains on human video, Generalist records people using hand-held grippers, and Physical Intelligence trains across robots and adds practice. Persona's proposed path starts with expert welders using its own platform at work sites. These choices determine what each company gets to observe and what progress it can measure.

The July weld shows the platform working together

With that control division in mind, the public welding demonstration becomes easier to read. Persona's First Spark post of July 8, 2026 places a humanoid at ARC Specialties, a welding automation shop in Houston. In the company-supplied sequence it walks to the workstation, squats, strikes an arc and runs a weld, then stands under its own power and walks away. It is untethered, with no gantry and no fixture holding the torch.

Persona describes the squat/weld/stand wide shot as continuous and unmodified, saying “what you see is what happened”. Read the operator and robot together when watching it. An expert is controlling the weld while the machine supports the motion with its own balance, footing and perception. The result shows a coordinated platform for expert operation in a live shop. Persona's posts disagree about the machine's generation, calling it Gen 1 in First Spark and Gen 2 in the skilled-trades account, so I refer to it here as a Persona humanoid.

The squat matters to the earlier site-access argument. The robot gets its body into a working position, uses a tool, and leaves under its own power. The recording also belongs in the learning loop just described.

Partners supply the conditions the robot must learn

A shop demonstration needs a path into customer work. Persona's partnerships supply different parts of that path. The Korea Times reports a May 2025 memorandum of understanding followed by a March 2026 joint-development agreement with HD Korea Shipbuilding and Offshore Engineering, abbreviated HD KSOE, and HD Hyundai Robotics. The shipbuilder contributes training data and the robotics affiliate handles deployment. Seoul Economic Daily reported proofs of concept with HD Hyundai and POSCO DX in September 2026. Those relationships are in development and proof-of-concept stages.

POSCO, described in Persona's account as one of the world's largest steel producers, brings steel-site logistics into the work. Its DX affiliate is also an investor, with a reported $2 million investment in December 2025. These are useful connections for defining industrial tasks and their surroundings.

A smaller workplace gives the initial weld a more immediate setting. SSE Steel Fabrication is a Louisiana business making bespoke structural steel, with about 75 people. The company's pilot summary describes a 5 ft 8 in robot with two arms and two legs, able to walk stairs and use the crew's tools. The pilot anticipated arrival during 2026 for fillet welding on the live production floor. Cameras had already recorded the floor for months to help build a digital twin and simulation before the robot's attempt. Persona's digital-twin account describes this preparation more generally for customer sites.

Persona's summary of The Fabricator expects a robot on the floor “within a couple of years”, introduced gradually. The two summaries give different arrival forecasts. Cameras and a simulated shop give the team a way to prepare for the surroundings; the machine still has to weld in the real production workflow.

The remaining partner badges on the board address conditions around that work. ABS is involved in class and safety standards, a relationship that precedes any established certification in this record. Under Armour's collaboration studies performance materials and workwear under industrial wear. Persona explicitly calls it “this is research, not a product”. The yard needs a machine that can keep working in its surroundings, and these relationships put requirements beyond arm motion into development.

The team is building toward that job with substantial prior robotics experience. Radford led NASA's Valkyrie program and founded Nauticus Robotics. Pratt led IHMC's DARPA Robotics Challenge team and spent a couple of years as Figure's CTO. Their founding account in IEEE describes a broad search in 2024. They considered warehousing and automotive work, and also explored homes, before settling on skilled trades and tool use. Radford calls the benefit of learning from earlier entrants “last-mover advantage”. He also recounts being told Persona wasn't thinking big enough. Pratt sees many technical problems shared by homes and shipyards, and credits strong teams across the field with making progress.

Founded in June 2024, Persona is about two years old at this article's October 26, 2026 snapshot. Its hiring points toward making and supporting machines as well as developing them. Brian Davis became head of global manufacturing after experience at Amazon Robotics and Dell. Michael Perry became head of commercial strategy with a background at Boston Dynamics and DJI. The company reports Gen 3 units already on the ground and a presentation planned for fall 2026. Those are reported hardware and unveiling milestones.

Measure independent work and repeated usefulness

The board's status panel separates shown or reported steps from unpublished outcomes. Its green marks include the teleoperated weld, partner agreements, reported Gen 3 units and money sold in an offering. Its red marks identify gaps in the cited public record. As of this snapshot, that record provides no published autonomous-welding result, whole production shift, hundreds of units at one site, or Persona pricing, margins and profit. The demonstrations and business readiness require separate measurements.

Capital helps explain the capacity to pursue the plan. Persona's September 14, 2026 Form D records about $65.4 million sold within an approximately $142 million offering. The offering's exact amounts and earlier financing reports are in the source notes. Funding pays for development; an offering amount sold measures financing. Customer usefulness has to be established through the work.

The broader market is still heavily populated by pilots in the cited reporting. Seoul Economic Daily relays an International Federation of Robotics estimate of about 7,000 industrial and professional-service humanoids sold worldwide in 2025, mostly pilots. That second-hand number helps explain why a partnership announcement needs a task-level follow-up. For our seam, I'd want an autonomous weld accompanied by the number of attempts and the number completed successfully. A continuous teleoperated shot gives us a different observation.

Watch the seam become dependable capacity

My preference for Persona's initial job comes from how the pieces fit. A yard unable to hire enough people values additional production. Human tools and human access routes connect the robot's body to the cost of putting it to work. A common linear weld gives expert demonstrations a bounded skill to teach. The choices give the company a practical way to discover whether its machine can earn a place in a customer's workflow.

I'd watch for the autonomous weld with trial counts first, then repeated useful operation through a shift. After that, the service economics become assessable through the cost of keeping the robot working and the output the customer gains. Follow the same seam through those milestones, until the yard can schedule dependable additional welding capacity against an order it needs to finish.

Sources and the details behind the figures

The sources below were published by October 26, 2026.

The interviews explain the choice of work

Evan Ackerman's August 17, 2026 IEEE Spectrum feature appears under the titles “Is Shipyard Welding the Right First Job for Humanoid Robots?” and “How Persona AI Makes Humanoids Pay Off In Welding”. It supplies the founder histories, welding constraints, customer reasoning, yard-access account and planned demonstration scale used here. Radford describes the company's early search as broad; his phrase was “we were all over the place”. His account of critics was “we're not thinking big enough”. Pratt describes overlap in the technical problems across home and industrial settings and praises the field's teams. These are interview judgments. The August feature names HD Hyundai and POSCO as its two public partnerships.

Persona's founding account and the February 2025 InnovationMap interview describe a Houston company founded in June 2024 by three co-founders, with the third serving as COO. The Form D records Delaware incorporation in 2024. Persona's homepage, lease page and skilled-trades article are primary statements of company positioning and intended work.

Financing reports describe different quantities

In InnovationMap on February 5, 2025, Radford reports eight figures, more than $10 million, in pre-seed funding from investors in the US, London and Singapore. That is the interview basis for the board's $10M+ label. The same report gives a delivery forecast of 18 to 24 months from that date.

RoboHorizon, December 31, 2025, calls the funding around the December Gen 1 unveiling “$42 million in pre-seed funding”. It describes a tendon-driven hand and an office in Pensacola. That financing figure has no independent filing confirmation in this record. Asia Economy, December 23, 2025, reports POSCO DX's $2 million investment, also discussed in Persona's Korean account and Seoul Economic Daily. POSCO is a collaborator and investor; DX is the affiliate named for this investment.

The Persona AI Inc. Form D filed September 14, 2026 lists an offering of $141,964,814, with $65,363,626 sold and $76,601,188 remaining, and a first sale on August 28, 2026. The board rounds the offering to $142M and the amount sold to $65.4M. These quantities belong within this offering and are separate from the earlier financing history; adding the reports would produce an unsupported cumulative total.

Workforce estimates have separate horizons

Biz New Orleans relays the American Welding Society's roughly 82,500 annual US welding positions through 2029 and the estimates of age 55 and two entrants per five retirees. Its relay of a Deloitte/Manufacturing Institute study gives up to 3.8 million new US manufacturing workers needed by 2033, with about 1.9 million positions potentially unfilled.

The 2.1 million US manufacturing vacancies projected for 2030 comes through Persona's Korean manufacturing account, Seoul Economic Daily and Persona's commercial-strategy account. It has a different horizon from the 2033 estimate. Seoul Economic Daily attributes to Michael Perry a projected US shortage of more than 330,000 welders by 2028.

The roughly 40,000 skilled-worker shortage in North American and Korean shipbuilding is Persona's figure in its skilled-trades and Korean accounts, including its summary of IEEE's feature. Maekyung's April 2026 interview also quotes Radford on the roughly 40,000-worker shortfall. Persona's Korean account supplies Ulsan's 48.3 mean age and the report of yards turning down orders. The underlying AWS, Deloitte/Manufacturing Institute and other labor reports were not verified.

The partner accounts describe work in development

The March 23, 2026 Korea Times report establishes the May 2025 memorandum and subsequent joint-development agreement. Seoul Economic Daily, September 22, 2026, reports the HD Hyundai and POSCO DX proofs of concept and ambitions in energy and construction after shipbuilding. Its forecast says “robots will be commercialized on manufacturing floors two years from now”, dating that expectation to September 2026. It also attributes the roughly 7,000 worldwide industrial/professional-service humanoid sales in 2025, mostly pilots, to the International Federation of Robotics. The underlying IFR source wasn't verified.

Biz New Orleans reports about 75 SSE employees and roughly $30 million in annual revenue. Persona's summary supplies the robot dimensions, stair walking and crew-tool use. Its Fabricator summary gives 300 to 800 tons per month, without specifying the ton convention. The original Fabricator article was unreachable, so its shop-floor quotations and tonnage are cited through Persona.

ABS's class and safety role comes through Persona's skilled-trades account and IEEE. The Under Armour announcement is a primary company account of materials research. Persona's customer-site digital-twin article supplies the simulation context. The company reports Gen 3 units on the ground and a fall 2026 presentation in its Korean account, also relayed by Seoul Economic Daily; these are reported hardware milestones.

Persona reports the weld and comments on industrial support

The July 8 First Spark post and the August 6 teleoperation article are Persona's own descriptions.

Persona's FCC account relays Ackerman's IEEE coverage of the July 2026 mobile-robot ruling as restricting new foreign-built mobile robots. The regulatory scope remains unverified here. Radford comments on auditability, fast support and resilient supply chains. My inference is that audit and service capability matter commercially for a Houston supplier serving American and Korean heavy industry.

The comparison keeps each company's evidence in its own units

Agility's October 26, 2026 statement calls its June 2024 deployment the first formal commercial humanoid deployment in live operations, a company firstness claim. Its 100,000-plus GXO tote count covers the agreement begun that month. The reported 65,000 operating hours cover commercial operations and customer programs. The statement also mentions RoboFab in Salem and a combination with Churchill Capital Corp XI. Its conditional $300 million-plus Digit 5 order commitment is an order measure.

The 1X company account puts NEO in early-access homes on its 2025 and 2026 timeline and describes living and learning alongside people. 1X describes its choice as “1X bets on the home”. The $200 on the NEO page is a reservation deposit.

Apptronik's mission identifies dull, dirty and dangerous industrial tasks. Its announcement record supplies the Mercedes-Benz and GXO pilots, Jabil manufacturing relationship, December 2024 Google DeepMind partnership, March 2025 $403 million Series A, and June 2026 Robot Park announcement. Robot Park fleets collect Apollo data with DeepMind.

Tesla's row rests on its FY2025 Form 10-K, which describes a general-purpose autonomous humanoid in development and says “we intend to leverage our current operations”. Tesla's website was unreachable in the earlier research. Figure's site and the companion discussion supply its homes-and-factories framing and the body/learning comparison with Generalist and Physical Intelligence.

No source in this comparison supplies robot prices.
